newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish toy firm says business not child's play.
newsitem.headline: Swedish toy firm says business not child's play.

text.p: Sweden's Brio, known for its simple but loved wooden toys, said on Friday it plans to target overseas markets with its high-quality products and maybe even make some acquisitions.
But Brio has seen profits slashed as it struggles to cope with the loss of partner U.S. toy maker Hasbro and low birth rates in Sweden which have hit sales of prams, a key product.

With already over 90 percent of the company's pretty wooden toys -- the company is best known for its beech wood, brightly coloured trains -- made for export, Brio is a well known name among discerning parents.
The company also manufactures prams, mostly for the Swedish market, and is a toy distributor in the Nordic region.

After announcing a licensing agreement this week with Finnish textile company Reima-Tutta to manufacture and sell children's clothing and shoes, Brio Managing Director Bengt Ivarsson said he would consider other partnerships or purchases.

"We're always looking around, but it has to do with if the company is the right one for us, and if the price is right," Ivarsson told Reuters in an interview. "I haven't seen anyone that really fits into that."

The Brio group also said this week it bought the Plasto toy unit of Finnish potato chip and toy group Ab Chips Oy Ltd for an undisclosed sum, expected to add around 100 million crowns ($14.6 million) to the company's turnover.

Brio, whose name stands for Brothers Ivarsson & Osby, was started over 100 years ago by Ivarsson's great grandfather. The first toy the company made was a small wooden horse similar to those still sold in Swedish shops.
Of its own production, which makes up about one-third of its turnover, its trademark wooden toys account for about 70 percent. Around half are exported to the U.S..

After an unsuccessful link last year with an American licenser, Brio is actively looking for another partner to market children's products under the Brio name outside its own product line of toys, games and prams.
"We have a strong position (in the U.S.) although we only sell to speciality toy retailers there, not to the discount channels," Ivarsson said.

Since it was listed in 1985, Brio's operating income has nearly doubled to 1.44 billion crowns which it posted in 1995. Its pre-tax profit last year fell to 60.2 million crowns from 85 million crowns in 1994.
Although a low Swedish birth rate haunts Brio's pram division, the company said it has no plans to part with it.
"We have a saying -- children and Brio belong together...it's been profitable a lot of years. It's only this year that we've had some problems," Ivarsson said.
Instead Brio plans to step up marketing of its prams on the British and U.S. markets and expand its product range.
In 1996 Brio expects its result to be even worse, with pre-tax profit falling to about one-third of 1995 levels.

Brio said it is not interested in selling out to a foreign toy giant. "We're not for sale. We've been in this business 112 years and we're still mainly owned by the family and we intend to continue that way," Ivarsson said.

The company aims to find other licensing agents to use the Brio brand name, probably the company's most valuable asset, but partners must adhere to Brio's philosophy of developing products that benefit children.

During the 1950s Brio had a licensing agreement to make Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck toys out of wood and in the 1980s it supplied hit sellers such as board game Trivial Pursuit and My Little Pony figures and accessories in the Nordic region.
"We intend to continue with our basic philosophy and that's based on giving very good toys to children which develop their lives," Ivarsson said. ($ = 6.858 Swedish Crowns)
